title: System Design: Message Queue & Async Processing

card.intuition: A durable buffer that decouples producers from consumers: publishers enqueue messages, and workers consume them at their own pace. This lets you absorb traffic spikes, smooth bursty loads, retry failed work, and fan work out across many consumers.
card.analogy: A restaurant kitchen ticket rail: the chef (producer) fires a ticket onto the rail (queue), and multiple line cooks (consumers) pick up tickets as they finish their current dish. If a cook is slow, tickets pile up and wait rather than blocking the chef.
card.time_complexity: Enqueue and dequeue are amortized O(1) per message on the queue itself; end-to-end latency is bounded by consumer throughput and backlog.
card.space_complexity: Queue storage grows with the message backlog; un-consumed messages persist until acknowledged or they hit retention limits.
when_to_use: Decoupling a fast producer from slow or varying-rate consumers (e.g. email, image processing)
Absorbing load spikes so bursts don't crash downstream services
Implementing reliable, retryable async work and fan-out to multiple workers
gotchas: At-least-once delivery with auto-retries can produce duplicates — consumers must be idempotent
A dead-letter queue is essential: poison messages that crash workers must be quarantined, not retried forever

steps.annotation: Producers publish messages (events, jobs) into a named topic without waiting for a reply.
The queue durably stores messages, acting as a buffer that absorbs spikes in producer volume.
Consumers poll the queue and process messages at their own rate, acking each one on success.
Messages a consumer fails to process are retried; repeated failures land in a dead-letter queue.
Processing results fan back into the system, and throughput scales by adding more consumers.

exercise.prompt: A producer publishes 2,000 messages in a 5-second burst and consumers process 100 messages/second each. How many consumers are needed so the backlog is cleared in 4 seconds?
exercise.starter_code:
messages = 2000
rate_per_consumer = 100
seconds = 4

consumers = messages / (rate_per_consumer * seconds)
# Result is ___ consumers
exercise.test_code:
def check(ans):
    try: return int(ans) == 5
    except: return False
assert check("5")
print("PASS")
